title: Swapping the unspoken step
takeaway: Exchanging an unspoken intermediate concept for an alternative, purely in J-lens coordinates, changes the model's final answer to the one the swapped-in concept implies. Across three worked examples — a two-hop fact, a planned rhyme, and a cross-language antonym — the output tracks the substituted intermediate, which the paper takes as evidence that these lens vectors are causally load-bearing for internal reasoning, not just readable.
walkthrough:
In the published article this figure is an interactive widget rather than a static image; the ingest carries no picture of it. It collects three demonstrations of one intervention, one per row. Each row has three parts: a prompt whose correct answer depends on an intermediate concept the model never writes down, the [[lens-coordinate-swap]] applied to that concept (shown on the left), and the model's top-5 next-token log-probabilities in two side-by-side readouts — "clean" for the unmodified forward pass, "swapped" for the pass with the intervention in place.

The intervention operates on coordinates. Every vocabulary token has a [[j-lens-vector]], a direction in the [[residual-stream]]. The swap reads the activation's coordinates along the intermediate's vector and along a chosen alternative's vector, exchanges the two values, and writes the result back. The part of the activation orthogonal to those two directions is left untouched. Here the swap is also clamped: it is applied at every token position and held through the forward pass ([[activation-clamping]]), so the model cannot quietly recompute the original intermediate.

The first row is the prompt "The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is". Answering requires first inferring *spider*, a word absent from both prompt and output. With spider swapped for ant, the top next token moves from "8" to "6" — the leg count of an ant.

The second row is planning. After the line "The soldier marched into the night," the lens shows *fight* as the planned rhyme for the second line's end. Swapping fight for light changes the model's next word from "coming" to "morning", so the completion becomes "morning light". An intervention on a planned future word has altered earlier word choices ([[rhyme-planning]]).

The third row asks, in Chinese, for the antonym of 小 ("small"). The lens carries the English tokens *big* and *bigger* ([[shared-multilingual-representation]]). Swapping both for *long* and *longer* flips the Chinese output from 大 ("big") to 长 ("long").

In each row the new answer is the one the substituted intermediate implies, not a scrambled output. This is the figure's point, and the causal half of section 3.3's [[internal-reasoning]] claim. These are three chosen examples on the paper's default subject model, Sonnet 4.5; the systematic version, 50 two-hop prompts with 54–70% swap success across model sizes, is Figure 15.

terms.definition: The intervention each row applies: the activation's coordinates along two J-lens vectors — the true intermediate's and an alternative's — are read out with a pseudoinverse, exchanged, and written back, leaving everything orthogonal to those two directions unchanged.
The label on the left readout of each row: the model's top-5 next-token log-probabilities from an ordinary forward pass, with no intervention.
The label on the right readout of each row: the same top-5 next-token log-probabilities after the lens-coordinate swap has been applied and clamped at every position.
The five most probable next tokens in the model's output distribution, shown with their log-probabilities; the figure compares this list before and after the swap.

The swap is not applied once and released: the exchanged lens coordinates are held at their swapped values at every token position throughout the forward pass, so downstream layers cannot restore the original intermediate.

A concept the model must compute on the way to its answer but never writes in the prompt or the output — spider, the planned rhyme fight, or the English-language antonym big. Section 3.3 tests whether such intermediates live in the J-space and carry causal weight.
One direction in the residual stream per vocabulary token, produced by the Jacobian lens; the swap operates on the activation's coordinates along two of these vectors.
Row one's swap: the inferred animal behind "the animal that spins webs" is exchanged for ant, and the answer changes from a spider's leg count to an ant's.
Row two's swap: the planned rhyme word for the couplet's second line is exchanged, changing the model's word choices before the line's end and the final rhyme.
Row three's swap: two English lens tokens carrying the antonym intermediate are exchanged for long and longer, redirecting the Chinese output accordingly.
The Chinese tokens of row three: the prompt asks for the antonym of 小 ("small"); the clean answer is 大 ("big"); after the swap the answer is 长 ("long").
The model's next word in the couplet's second line before and after the rhyme swap; the change happens several tokens before the rhyme word itself is written.
The paper's default subject model, a mid-size production Claude model; section 2.5 states that results are reported on it unless noted otherwise.

numbers.meaning: The number of rows: a two-hop factual prompt (spider), a rhyme-planning prompt (fight), and a Chinese antonym prompt (big). Each demonstrates the same swap-and-observe procedure on a different kind of unspoken intermediate.
Each readout shows the top 5 tokens of the model's next-token distribution with their log-probabilities — enough to see the old answer displaced and the new one on top.

Each swap involves exactly two J-lens vectors, the source concept's and the target's; only the activation's coordinates along these two directions are modified. Row three is the exception in swapping two token pairs (big→long and bigger→longer), because the intermediate surfaces as both tokens.

Row one's output change: 8 is the number of legs on a spider, the clean answer; 6 is the number of legs on an ant, the answer implied by the swapped-in intermediate. The consistency of the new answer with the new intermediate is what makes the swap evidence of mediation.
The swap is applied and clamped at all token positions of the prompt, not at one chosen site, so the intermediate is exchanged wherever it is represented.

Not printed in this figure but the systematic counterpart of it (Figure 15): over 50 two-hop prompts, the swap moves the target-appropriate answer to top-1 on 54% of trials for Haiku 4.5 and 70% for Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5. The three rows here are individual worked examples of that procedure.
